name: Alfacalcidol (an active vitamin D medicine)
short: Kidney injury: Japanese reports (alfacalcidol reporting odds ratio 5.29), case series, an overdose with very high calcium. Calcitriol/alfacalcidol trial review: more hypercalcaemia (odds ratio 3.63).
text: Alfacalcidol is an active form of vitamin D that, as one abstract notes, is commonly prescribed for osteoporosis; these data are for the medicine (where the cited trials and reviews give a route, it was taken by mouth), not ordinary vitamin D supplements. The main harms reported in the cited sources are kidney injury and high blood calcium. In a pharmacovigilance study of the Japanese Adverse Drug Event Report database (298,891 reports, 2004 to 2023), acute kidney injury was significantly associated with active vitamin D3 analogues, including alfacalcidol (reporting odds ratio 5.29); onset came a median of 15.4 weeks after starting, and the risk was higher with age 70 or over, weight under 50 kg, high blood pressure and use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or magnesium oxide; the authors advise prescribers to consider kidney injury in patients with these risk factors, especially in the first 6 months. In a retrospective case series of 23 adults with severe motor and intellectual disabilities, 6 of 16 showed a fall in kidney function of 30% or more while taking alfacalcidol, and in the 11 who stopped it, median eGFR rose significantly from 43.0 to 65.1 mL/min/1.73 m2. In a case report, a woman who accidentally took four times her usual alfacalcidol dose for several weeks developed very high blood calcium (16.7 mg/dL), acute kidney injury, severe high blood pressure and anaemia, which recovered after calcium and alfacalcidol were stopped. In a 48-month open-label trial in 976 people on haemodialysis, alfacalcidol by mouth numerically, but not significantly, increased cardiovascular events. Reviews of trials also report high blood calcium. A 2008 systematic review of 23 randomised trials (2,139 participants) of calcitriol or alfacalcidol for fractures and falls, compared with placebo or calcium, 16 of which had enough data for meta-analysis, found an increased risk of hypercalcaemia (high blood calcium; odds ratio 3.63) and a trend towards more hypercalciuria (high urine calcium), which it calls potential side effects; the abstract does not give this risk separately for each medicine. A 2021 meta-analysis of six placebo-controlled trials of active vitamin D taken by mouth, in 799 adults with chronic kidney disease not on dialysis and with secondary hyperparathyroidism (five trials of paricalcitol and one of alfacalcidol), found hypercalcaemia 6.6 times more likely than with placebo (odds ratio 6.63). On the other side, in an 18-month double-blind trial in 148 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, adverse events and blood calcium were similar with alfacalcidol and with vitamin D plus calcium, and the authors of a 12-week placebo-controlled trial in 77 people with chronic urticaria conclude that there were no reported side effects; the abstract gives no adverse-event numbers. Interactions: in the Japanese database study, concurrent non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and magnesium oxide were associated with acute kidney injury.
